rationale: CRC stool is marked by a group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is rare and sparse, so a random forest struggles to split on any of them alone. This change adds three features built from taxonomy names: their pooled log abundance, how many of them are detected, and log(oral load / butyrate producers). These should give the forest a strong combined signal and should also carry over to the external studies.

Baxter's CRC signal comes mostly from a few low-abundance oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). In a random forest built on about 200 genus features, each of these sparse genera is offered to only a few splits, so the signal gets diluted. This change adds summary features for that marker set: how many markers are present, the log of their pooled relative abundance, and the maximum single-marker abundance. These features use taxonomy names only, so they should carry over to the external CRC studies. I haven't run this here, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

The strongest CRC signal in stool is a small group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and noisy alone, and a random forest that tries about 14 of roughly 200 genera per split rarely picks any of them. I add two composite marker features built from taxonomy names: the log total relative abundance of these genera and how many of them are detected. Because they use names rather than study-specific OTU ids, they should also carry over to the external CRC studies.

CRC stool has a consistent signal of oral pathobionts that are usually found together (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas). Each one is sparse and low in abundance, so a random forest that splits on one genus at a time picks up the shared signal poorly. I'm adding two summary features built from taxonomy names: the log of their combined relative abundance, and how many of the four are detected. Because they use names rather than OTU ids, they should carry over to the external studies.

I'm replacing genus relative abundances with centered log-ratio (CLR) transformed genus counts, using a pseudocount of 0.5. Relative abundances are compositional and squash the rare CRC-associated oral taxa (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas) to near zero, and they vary with sequencing depth. CLR puts the features on a log scale, centred within each sample, so the random forest's splits pick up those low-abundance signals. It still uses taxonomy names only, so it should transfer to the other studies.

CRC's strongest stool signal is a group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas, Gemella) that tend to appear together. Each one is sparse and low-abundance, so a random forest has trouble splitting on them one at a time. I add combined features — summed log-abundance, number of marker genera present, and one log-abundance per marker — built from taxonomy names, so they carry over to the external CRC studies.

CRC's most reproducible 16S signal is a group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and often present only at low abundance. A random forest that sees each genus separately gets only a weak, noisy split from any one of them, so I'm adding a composite "oral-pathogen" log-abundance score and a count of how many of these genera are detected. These are taxonomy-name features, so they should also carry over to the four external CRC studies.

CRC stool in Baxter 2016 is marked by a small group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas). These are usually present at low abundance, and a random forest spread over about 300 genera tends to dilute their signal. This change adds a fixed, label-free marker score: the sum of log10 relative abundances of those genera, with a pseudocount. The final prediction is the average of that score's rank and the RF probability's rank. The score uses genus names only, so it should carry over to the external CRC studies.

The main CRC signal in Baxter 2016 comes from a few rare oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas). They are present in very few samples, so a random forest choosing among roughly 300 genera rarely splits on them. I'm adding a few features that pool these taxa into one oral-pathogen score (their summed log abundance, how many of them are detected, and their total abundance), which gives the forest one strong feature to split on. Because the features are built from taxonomy names, they should also carry over to the external CRC studies.

These give a denser signal than any single genus, and because they are built from taxonomy names they should carry over to the external CRC studies.

Each is sparse and gets lost among ~200 genera in a random forest. So I add two summary features built from taxonomy names: a combined log-abundance score and a count of how many of these genera are present. CRC stool signatures are dominated by a group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas/Micromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and low-abundance, so an RF splitting on single genera picks up their signal only weakly. This change adds summed "oral-pathogen" features to the genus table: the total log abundance and a count of how many marker genera are present. Because they are built from taxonomy names, they should also carry over to the external CRC studies.

My hypothesis is that most of the few hundred genera are rare or study-specific noise. In a random forest using `max_features=sqrt`, those noise genera fill most of each split's candidate features, so low-abundance CRC markers like Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas and Porphyromonas are rarely picked. This version keeps only genera present (>0 reads) in at least 10% of the training-fold samples, computed without labels inside `fit_predict`. That should let the forest focus on informative taxa and transfer better to other studies.

CRC-associated oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas) are rare and patchy in stool. A random forest that samples about √300 genera per split rarely picks them up, so their combined signal gets diluted. I'm adding two features built from taxonomy names: the log of their summed abundance and how many of them are present. These give the forest a direct, study-agnostic biomarker that should also carry over to the external CRC studies. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.
